name: strings
one_line: print the printable character sequences in files
plain: `strings` scans a file and prints every run of readable text it finds (by default four or more characters long). Programs, images, memory dumps and archives all hide readable text among their bytes.
It is one of the fastest ways to see what a program mentions: file names, error messages, passwords, URLs and flags.
when: First look at an unknown binary: messages, paths, hard-coded passwords.
Search a memory dump or disk image for a keyword.
Find text appended to a picture or document.

examples.title: Windows (UTF-16) text hides from plain strings  (-e l)
examples.cmd: printf 'p\0a\0s\0s\0w\0o\0r\0d\0' > wide.bin; strings wide.bin; echo '--- with -e l:'; strings -e l wide.bin

options.plain: Scan the whole file, not just the data sections of a program. This is already the default in current versions.
options.use: Be sure you did not skip hidden regions.

options.plain: Scan only the initialised data sections of object files.
options.use: Skipping code and focusing on constants.

options.plain: Print the file name before each string.
Show only strings at least this many characters long (default 4).
options.use: Cut the noise: 8 or more is a good start.

options.plain: Same as -t o: print each string's offset in octal.
Print each string's offset in decimal (d), octal (o) or hexadecimal (x).
options.use: Locating the text so you can open it with xxd -s.

options.plain: Which kind of characters to look for: s (single 7-bit bytes, default), S (single 8-bit), b/l (16-bit big/little endian), B/L (32-bit big/little endian).
Put this string between results instead of a newline.
Count all whitespace (tabs, spaces, line breaks) as part of a string.
Specify the file format instead of auto-detecting it.
How to treat UTF-8 characters: default, invalid, locale, escape, hex or highlight.
options.use: Seeing odd characters in the text.

options.plain: Print a short usage message and exit.

mistakes: Looking only at the first screen: pipe through grep or less.
Forgetting UTF-16 (-e l) for Windows files and memory images.
Assuming that no strings means nothing is there: data may be compressed, encrypted or encoded.
Running strings on huge files without -n: the output is endless.
try: Find the secret passphrase in hello with strings and run the program with it.
Find which offset the flag text sits at in pic.png and look at the bytes there.
Make a small UTF-16 file and compare strings with and without -e l.
Pipe strings of a large file through sort | uniq -c | sort -rn and look at the top lines.
see_also: grep(1) (-a and -b), xxd(1), file(1), od(1), binwalk(1) for files hidden inside files, floss for obfuscated strings.
